title: Runway checklist and terraform notes for bare‑metal ⇄ vSphere cluster init
body:
Purpose and scope:
This working note captures a pragmatic "runway" workflow for delivering on‑prem Kubernetes clusters where customers require a hybrid flow: some nodes provisioned on vSphere (VMs) while others are physical bare‑metal. The runbook focuses on the preflight checklist, deterministic order of operations, Terraform module conventions we found reliable, and clear upgrade + rollback heuristics.

High‑level runway phases (mnemonic: TAXI → LIFT → CRUISE → RETURN):
- TAXI: Preflight and inventory — hardware sanity, network segmentation, DNS, BMC reachability, template library verification.
- LIFT: Provision control plane (first 3 nodes), validate control plane quorum, bootstrap control plane services (etcd/CSI/CNI).
- CRUISE: Add workers, enable autoscaling pools (if using Dedicated), tune batching/latency defaults in runtime.
- RETURN: Planned upgrade/rollback path and post‑install telemetry hardening.

Preflight (TAXI) checklist — must pass before any infra apply:
- Hardware inventory CSV present and validated: mac, bmc_ip, model, expected NIC drivers.
- BMC credentials rotated into secrets manager; test ipmi/drac/redfish reachability and out‑of‑band power cycle. Example: ipmitool -I lanplus -H $BMC -U admin -P '***' chassis power status.
- vSphere content library: verify cluster VM template checksum and guest customization spec. Use govc to validate: GOVC_URL=... govc library.ls -json | jq .
- DNS: control-plane.<site>.internal pointed to the static VIP or external LB. Check wildcard entries for kubelets if using pod hostnames.
- NTP: All nodes and BMCs must sync; check with timedatectl status.
- Boot media tested: iPXE chain, factory ISO idempotence, and Ignition/cloud‑init conversion for target OS (Flatcar vs Ubuntu).
- Storage: NVMe/RAID controllers audited; identify controllers that require firmware downgrade to be stable during large disk churn.
- Network: MTU, SR‑IOV policies, and VLAN mapping approved; provide validated CNI MTU in the runbook.

Reliable LIFT sequence (control plane first):
1) Create or assign the control plane VIP and ensure HAProxy/MetalLB or vSphere LB is configured.
2) Bring up first control node (VM or baremetal) with minimal services. Wait for kubelet registration.
3) Create etcd cluster using static pods or operator; verify cluster healthy with etcdctl endpoint status.
4) Apply critical addons (CNI, CSI, storageclasses) in conservative mode (no auto scale).
5) Incrementally add control plane nodes 2→3 with quiescent intervals (10–15m) to allow leader election and snapshotting.

Node registration guidance (CRUISE):
- Workers must join with a per‑site bootstrap token (rotate after join). Keep join logs for 72h.
- For heterogeneous fleets: prefer labeling strategy and node pools in Terraform (worker_pool_type = [baremetal,cpu_optimized,gpu]).
- If vSphere VMs: prefer guest customization for cloud‑init that includes a late‑join script that verifies kubelet CA fingerprint before starting.

Terraform module notes — practical decisions and patterns we use:
- Module topology: module.cluster (orchestrates) ➜ module.compute_pool[*] (per pool) ➜ module.node_bootstrap. Keep each module small and idempotent.
- Use explicit depends_on for ordering where API emitters are eventual (e.g., wait for vsphere::vm.guest_net to report mac before provisioning DNS).
- Provider pinning: terraform { required_providers { vsphere = { source = "hashicorp/vsphere" version = ">=2.6.0, <3.0.0" } } } — we observed vsphere 3.x has API surface changes breaking older templates.
- Lifecycle: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [ "guest_id", "resource_pool_id" ] } for vSphere VMs to avoid churn from guest customization.
- Local exec and null_resource hacks: keep them in a separate module 'provisioner' and avoid mixing with core compute resources (makes plan readable).
- State partitioning: keep vSphere inventory state separate from cluster state to reduce blast radius. Use remote state with lock (GCS/S3 + Dynamo/Memcache).
- Variables: prefer explicit variables instead of maps for core bootstrap values to make drift reviews easier. Example variables used: control_count, worker_pools (list of objects), ipxe_base_url, ignition_bucket, bmc_credential_secret_id.
- Outputs: control_plane_ips, vsphere_vm_ids (list), bootstrap_token_id. Provide both machine-readable and human-readable outputs.
- Idempotency notes: when using content library templates, always version the template name and include checksum var. Example: template_name = "rwinf-ubuntu-22-04-tpl-v202511" and template_checksum = "sha256:..."

Common terraform pitfalls and mitigations:
- Race on DNS + VIP assignment: add a preflight remote_exec checks that resolves control plane VIP before creating kubeadm cluster.
- BMC secrets in state: never store raw BMC passwords in terraform state; refer to secret manager id and use external provider to fetch during apply.
- vSphere API throttling: add backoff/retry in provider config; split large jobs into batches.
- Template mismatches across tenants: ensure template customization scripts are idempotent (use marker files: /var/lib/infra/initialized).

Upgrade plan (minor and patch) — safe path:
- Preparation: capture cluster snapshot (etcd snapshot) and copy to a remote archive. Tag terraform state with a release tag.
- Canary: pick one worker pool and upgrade 10% of nodes. Verify CNI, admission webhooks, and user load tests.
- Control plane: upgrade control plane one node at a time. After each node: kube-apiserver logs dry run and a small e2e smoke test (api GET /healthz ; list pods in kube-system).
- Worker roll: drain one worker at a time with node‑graceful options and disruption budgets respected.
- Post‑upgrade: run a small set of quality checks (image pull, CSI attach/detach, persistent volume claims).

Rollback heuristics and emergency RETURN flow:
- If control plane fails to form quorum after an upgrade step, do not proceed. Revert the last change (apply terraform with previous template version) and restore etcd from snapshot.
- If a worker pool upgrade causes widespread pod evictions > disruption budget, pause and roll back that pool only.
- Always collect a debug bundle before any destructive rollback (kubectl cluster-info dump + journalctl from affected nodes).

Instrumenting for observability during run:
- Enable node and kubelet level metrics collection pre‑install; set alerting thresholds for etcd follower lag and apiserver request latency.
- Keep an ephemeral traces bucket for the run (30d retention) and upload kubeadm/journal bundles there.

Hardware and driver quirks worth calling out (site anecdotes):
- Broadcom iSCSI NICs where firmware mismatches cause kernel panic on large pod churn — vendor recommends firmware X.Y.Z.
- NVMe controller heat throttling on racks with poor airflow — prefer smaller disk IO tests during initial bootstrap (fio with 1G sample).
- Mellanox NICs on older kernels: lock to MLNX_OFED version known stable; test SR‑IOV detach cycles.

vSphere specific tips:
- Use govc for scripting: use govc vm.info -json to confirm guest network MACs to match inventory.
- Customization spec timezone and locale issues can break cloud‑init parsing — use a minimal spec that defers to cloud‑init for hostname and user-data.
- When backing up templates: snapshot the VM, then export to content library. Keep a template manifest with checksum and build timestamp.

Quick troubleshooting snippets (copy into incident doc):
- Check etcd health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=$EP endpoint status --write-out=table
- Confirm kubelet CA: openssl s_client -connect $NODE:10250 -showcerts | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint
- BMC power cycle via ipmitool: ipmitool -I lanplus -H $BMC -U $USER -P '***' chassis power cycle

Open questions / follow ups to convert into tickets:
- Should we standardize on Flatcar vs Ubuntu for all on‑prem clusters (tradeoffs around ignition vs cloud‑init)?
- Automated firmware validation step integrated into preflight (tooling + which vendors to support first).
- Tighten the Terraform module interface to return a single machine readable bootstrap manifest for operator consumption.

Appendix: suggested terraform variable checklist (for module authors) as comma separated values to copy into module README:
- control_count, control_cpu, control_memory_mb, worker_pools (list), pool_instance_type, pool_disk_size_gb, bmc_secret_ref, ipxe_image_base, ignition_bucket, vsphere_datacenter, vsphere_datastore, vsphere_network, template_name, template_checksum, content_library_id

Notes to reader: this is a working runbook — treat as a pragmatic checklist rather than policy. Comments welcome; send PRs to infra-modules repo and link test results to the confluence page in linked_artifacts.
